introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture), P52, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are expected to answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively.

Each essay must contain:
- An introduction = 5 marks
- A thesis = 7 marks
- An antithesis = 6 marks
- A synthesis = 3 marks
- A conclusion = 4 marks

Each question carries 25 marks.

Candidates are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of material.
incertitudes: Regle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR (04) questions chosen from the three sections imperatively » (quatre questions au total, prises dans les trois sections, donc au moins une par section). `regles_choix` porte ce minimum, une regle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section (Section One : questions 1-2 ; Section Two : questions 3-4 ; Section Three : questions 5-6) ; la regle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiee dans `introduction_markdown`. Le sujet ne dit pas explicitement « au moins une » ni si un candidat peut traiter les deux questions d'une meme section : c'est une lecture de « imperatively » et du total de quatre.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les criteres de la page de garde (introduction 5, these 7, antithese 6, synthese 3, conclusion 4 = 25) s'appliquent aux dissertations (questions 1 a 4) ; les corriges des dissertations suivent ce plan et indiquent les points par partie. Questions de texte (5 et 6) : a) 2 + 3 = 5, b) 4 (2 par expression, repartition choisie par le redacteur), c) 4, d) 4, e) 4, f) 4 = 25 ; aucun ecart de somme, aucun point corrige.

Aucun corrige officiel : les corriges sont des reponses modeles redigees de memoire, sans acces a une source. Les auteurs et positions cites sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie etablie, sans citation litterale, sans numero de page et sans date precise hors reperes de siecle et quelques dates admises (1945 Manchester, 1957 independance du Ghana, 1963 OUA, 2002 UA) ; a faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanne (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure ni tableau. Page de garde verifiee : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy, « Paper 2 (Philosophical Culture) », code 0790, P52, JUNE 2026, three hours. Intitule du paper et criteres recopies tels qu'imprimes (« Philosophical Culture », « imperatively », « Candidates are expected to »).

Q4 : positions attribuees de memoire (Tempels, Kagame, Mbiti ; critiques de Hountondji, Towa, Eboussi Boulaga, Wiredu ; Gyekye ; Oruka et la sagesse philosophique) sans citation ni titre precis ; le titre de Tempels est cite sous sa forme anglaise courante et date seulement des « annees 1940 ».

questions.enonce_markdown:
Is ethno-philosophy a justifiable philosophical trend?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction (5 marks).** *Ethno-philosophy* is the trend of African thought that presents the collective worldview, myths, proverbs, religion, language and customs of an African people as a philosophy. Its best-known early work is Placide Tempels' *Bantu Philosophy* (1940s), on the Luba of the Congo; other representatives include Alexis Kagame on the Banyarwanda and, in different ways, John Mbiti on African religions and the concept of time. Critics such as Paulin Hountondji, Marcien Towa, Kwasi Wiredu and Fabien Eboussi Boulaga have attacked it. The question is whether this trend is a *justifiable* philosophical enterprise, that is to say, whether it meets the standards of philosophy and serves a good purpose.

**Thesis: ethno-philosophy is justifiable (7 marks).**
- *It answers a colonial denial.* Colonial thinkers claimed that Africans had no philosophy and no developed thought. Ethno-philosophy answered that African societies had coherent views about being, the person, time, society and morality, and so defended the dignity of African culture.
- *Every philosophy grows from a culture.* Western philosophy started from Greek language and religion and from Christian and modern European experience. If these are accepted as the roots of philosophy, then the thought contained in African cultures can also be a starting point. Wiredu's and Gyekye's own work on Akan concepts of the person and of community shows that cultural material can support serious philosophical analysis.
- *Distinctive concepts.* It brought out ideas such as the primacy of the community, the "force" conception of being found by Tempels and Kagame, the idea of the person as formed through relations with others, and the cyclical or event-based sense of time discussed by Mbiti. These offer original perspectives for ethics, metaphysics and politics (for instance the idea of *ubuntu*).
- *Cultural identity and decolonisation.* The trend contributed to cultural nationalism and to Negritude, by providing material to rebuild identity after colonisation and to teach African ideas in African schools.
- *Preservation of oral tradition.* Africa's thought was transmitted orally; collecting and interpreting proverbs, myths and traditions preserves a heritage that would otherwise be lost.

**Antithesis: ethno-philosophy is not justified as philosophy (6 marks).**
- *Philosophy is critical and individual.* Hountondji argues that philosophy is a discipline of argument and criticism, written by identifiable individuals who give reasons for their views. Ethno-philosophy, by describing a collective and unanimous worldview, confuses philosophy with ethnography or folklore. He calls this assumption of unanimity "unanimism".
- *Projection of Western categories.* Tempels, a missionary, described Bantu thought with European concepts (being, force, causality), so critics say he wrote for a European audience and sometimes shaped his material to fit his own categories. Towa and Eboussi Boulaga add that the trend can serve colonial or missionary interests while pretending to defend Africans.
- *Static view of culture.* Treating "traditional thought" as fixed and common to all members of a people ignores disagreement, change and the internal critics who exist in every society. It may lead to an essentialism that locks Africans into a past.
- *No tests of truth.* Wiredu stresses that traditional beliefs must be examined by reason and evidence, as in any culture, and that mere description does not tell whether a view is true or justified; he also calls for "conceptual decolonisation", that is, an examination of inherited concepts.
- *Individual voices exist.* H. Odera Oruka's research on "sage philosophy" shows individual thinkers in traditional communities who criticise received opinions. This suggests that traditional Africa did not lack critical thought, and that ethno-philosophy hides it by giving only the collective view.

**Synthesis (3 marks).** The two sides can be reconciled. Ethno-philosophy is justified as a *source*: it records beliefs and concepts that can be material for philosophy, as Oruka and Gyekye recognise. It is not justified when it claims that the description itself is the philosophy or that all members of a society think alike. Philosophy begins when the material is analysed, compared, criticised and defended by arguments. The trend is thus acceptable as a first stage but insufficient as a complete philosophy.

**Conclusion (4 marks).** Ethno-philosophy is justifiable in part: it was a legitimate and historically important response to colonial denial, and it has preserved concepts valuable for later reflection. Yet as a philosophical method it is weak if it stays descriptive, collective and uncritical. The best view is that it should be kept as raw material and as a starting point, and completed by the critical, individual and argumentative work that Hountondji, Wiredu, Oruka and others demand.
